sub_answers.sub_question: Under what conditions of task orthogonality or high subspace overlap does overparameterization cease to reduce catastrophic forgetting?
sub_answers.text: Overparameterization ceases to reduce catastrophic forgetting when task updates concentrate along the same principal singular directions so that subspaces overlap strongly and protection of principal directions is required to avoid forgetting [d132209s0p0]. [d131842s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How do label distribution shifts, nonstationary input covariances, or adversarial task sequences undermine overparameterization benefits?
sub_answers.text: Non-stationary data streams and shifts in data distribution exacerbate catastrophic forgetting and undermine benefits from model overparameterization in online continual learning scenarios [d102169s0p0]. Label and modality shifts drive forgetting when tasks are modality- or task-type inconsistent, increasing the challenge for overparameterized models to retain previous abilities [d103483s0p0]. Larger models can exhibit increased forgetting during continual fine-tuning in some regimes, showing that scale alone does not immunize against distribution shifts or adversarial task sequences [d88015s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What are theoretical failure modes when optimization deviates from NTK-like dynamics in finite-width or non-linear settings?
sub_answers.text: Theoretical failure modes arise when optimization departs from NTK-like dynamics, because existing analyses that guarantee low forgetting often rely on linear, overparameterized, or NTK regimes and do not extend when finite-width or nonlinear training produces rich feature learning [d131842s0p0]. Different optimization dynamics such as non-convex concave min-max procedures can change convergence behavior so that overparameterization no longer ensures the same guarantees as in NTK-like settings [d66609s0p0]. The distinction between lazy and rich training regimes alters whether increasing width helps, so deviations toward feature-learning dynamics can invalidate overparameterization benefits [d110208s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What empirical counterexamples demonstrate that mere parameter count increase does not guarantee continual learning robustness?
sub_answers.text: Empirical studies show larger LLMs in the 1B–7B range can suffer more severe forgetting during continual instruction tuning, demonstrating that merely increasing parameter count does not guarantee continual learning robustness [d88015s0p0]. Fine-tuning recipes that concentrate updates along principal directions (standard SFT) remain susceptible to catastrophic forgetting even for large models unless subspace protection mechanisms are used [d132209s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How does task similarity or covariance structure between sequential tasks impact the benefits of overparameterization?
sub_answers.text:
High task similarity makes strong feature learning beneficial and reduces catastrophic forgetting compared to low-similarity sequences [d110208s0p0].
Task similarity explicitly enters forgetting bounds and affects the sign and magnitude of overparameterization benefits across objective classes [d131842s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What training protocols (e.g., learning rate schedules, batch sizes, single-pass vs multi-pass) interact with overparameterization effects?
sub_answers.text:
Learning-rate schedules (constant, intra-task decaying, and continuously decaying) materially change how perturbations propagate and thus interact with model parameterization effects on forgetting [d132661s0p0].
Single-pass (online) versus multi-pass training regimes change variance and final-risk behavior, with one-pass variance controlled by batching and multi-pass fluctuations differing from full-batch behavior [d124268s0p0].
Increasing model width benefits continual learning only when it induces a lazier (reduced feature-learning) regime; otherwise richer feature learning can increase forgetting [d110208s0p0].
Online single-pass continual learning intensifies catastrophic forgetting concerns addressed by overparameterization in theory and practice [d131842s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How does memory or rehearsal (e.g., replay buffers) complement or substitute for overparameterization in linear continual settings?
sub_answers.text:
Replay memory used with a generative classifier can bypass softmax logits bias and substantially reduce catastrophic forgetting in class-incremental online settings [d76272s0p0].
Representation rehearsal methods improve over raw image rehearsal and provide memory-efficient reductions in forgetting when combined with appropriate regularization and noise injections [d85175s0p0].
Sample-compression based retention of representative samples yields principled replay buffers that mitigate forgetting and permit computable generalization bounds in continual learning [d106358s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What are the observed scalability limits of overparameterization benefits with increasing number of tasks in empirical studies?
sub_answers.text:
Theoretical upper bounds on expected forgetting explicitly depend on the total number of tasks, indicating that forgetting increases with more tasks unless other quantities (like data per task or alignment) compensate [d132661s0p0].
Empirical neural-network experiments on Split-CIFAR-100 and Permuted-MNIST exhibit the same trends predicted by convex-theory analyses as task counts increase, showing limited transfer of overparameterization benefits across many tasks without additional mechanisms [d131842s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What is the definition of linear continual learning in the context of sequential task training?
sub_answers.text: Linear continual learning studies sequentially training linear predictors on a sequence of tasks where each task provides new training data and the learner updates parameters progressively via an optimizer such as SGD [d96673s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What is catastrophic forgetting and how is it quantified in linear models trained sequentially?
sub_answers.text: For linear models trained sequentially with SGD, forgetting is analyzed through changes in generalization loss after each task and through how task order and algorithmic parameters like step size affect that loss [d96673s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What empirical observations link model width or parameter count to forgetting in linear networks?
sub_answers.text: Simulations on linear regression models and deep networks were used to validate theoretical findings about forgetting across parameterization regimes [d96673s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What theoretical frameworks (e.g., NTK, linear regression analyses) describe overparameterization effects in linear models?
sub_answers.text: Another theoretical perspective analyzes the geometry of the parameter space after task training, describing regions near optima as cone-like and studying principal directions of optimizer trajectories to motivate constraints that reduce forgetting [d63301s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How does the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime characterize training dynamics of overparameterized linear and linearized models?
sub_answers.text:
The Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime characterizes training dynamics by linearizing the model around initialization so training follows a fixed kernel prediction dynamics rather than feature learning [d131842s0p0].
Linearized models can be described by a data-dependent Gram-induced kernel that governs generalization and training trajectories in place of nonlinear parameter updates [d120775s0p0].
Practical networks can behave in a lazy (NTK-like) or rich feature-learning regime, and the NTK description applies in the lazy regime and in certain infinite-width limits where feature changes are negligible [d110208s0p0].
The NTK limit can be unreachable at practical widths for some architectures, implying the kernel characterization may not hold in realistic finite-width linearized models [d120775s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How does increased parameter dimensionality affect solution multiplicity and projection onto task subspaces in linear regression?
sub_answers.text:
Increasing parameter dimensionality creates an overparameterized linear system that admits many global solutions, producing solution multiplicity in linear regression [d96673s0p0].
Overparameterization allows the learner to choose solutions by projecting onto task-relevant parameter subspaces or by constraining updates to lie in particular low-rank or orthogonal subspaces [d107377s0p0].
Architectures or parameterizations that allocate distinct subvectors or low-rank subspaces per task make it possible to localize solutions and reduce interference via per-subspace parameter updates [d89976s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What role do orthogonality and subspace overlap of task feature vectors play in interference mitigation?
sub_answers.text:
Orthogonality of task parameter subspaces reduces interference by keeping task updates in mutually orthogonal directions, thereby minimizing overlap in parameter changes between tasks [d89976s0p0].
Subspace overlap increases cross-task coupling in the effective kernel or NTK, which raises interference and forgetting by allowing updates for one task to alter the predictive directions for another [d123667s0p0].
Constraining updates to be orthogonal to critical directions of prior tasks prevents those directions from being changed and thus mitigates interference during subsequent training [d107377s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How does implicit bias of gradient descent in overparameterized linear models influence retention of earlier task solutions?
sub_answers.text:
The implicit bias of gradient descent in overparameterized linear models picks particular solutions among many, and this bias affects how much earlier-task solutions are preserved during continued training [d96673s0p0].
When training operates in a lazy/NTK-like regime with limited feature change, gradient dynamics tend to retain earlier task solutions better and produce lower forgetting [d110208s0p0].
Architectural or kernel structure that induces a rank deficit or reduced cross-task NTK coupling helps gradient descent implicitly preserve prior solutions and yields formal forgetting bounds [d123667s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: For what specific relationships between task representations (e.g., orthogonal vs. partially overlapping feature subspaces, cosine similarity thresholds, rank of shared subspace) does increasing model size stop improving resistance to catastrophic forgetting?
sub_answers.text: Increasing model width stops improving resistance to catastrophic forgetting when the model transitions out of an effectively lazy regime into a rich feature-learning regime driven by task dissimilarity, causing significant forgetting [d110208s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: In what ways do shifts in class priors, time-varying input covariance matrices, or intentionally adversarially ordered tasks (e.g., frequent label permutation, covariate shift schedules) negate the continual-learning advantages of large overparameterized networks?
sub_answers.text: High task non-stationarity and low task similarity negate the continual-learning advantages of large overparameterized networks by promoting rich feature learning that amplifies forgetting despite scale [d110208s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which formal conditions and examples show optimization trajectories departing from Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) behavior—such as strong feature learning, large learning rates, or finite-width effects—lead to theoretical breakdowns of overparameterization-based forgetting guarantees?
sub_answers.text: Formal conditions showing breakdowns of NTK-based guarantees include strong feature learning and departures from the lazy limit that arise at finite width, where optimization dynamics leave the NTK regime and provably allow greater forgetting [d110208s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What published experiments or benchmark results (datasets, model widths, training regimes) provide concrete counterexamples where simply increasing parameter count fails to improve, or worsens, continual learning performance compared to smaller models?
sub_answers.text: Systematic empirical studies demonstrate that simply increasing model width does not always reduce forgetting and can fail when increased width induces richer feature learning under non-stationary tasks, producing a transition to higher forgetting; these conclusions arise from controlled experiments contrasting lazy and feature-learning regimes across scales [d110208s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How do specific measures of task similarity (e.g., task covariance matrices, alignment of task subspaces, principal angle distributions, and eigenvalue spectra) quantitatively change the magnitude of benefits from increasing model width in sequential-task linear models?
sub_answers.text: Increasing model width is beneficial only when it reduces the amount of feature learning and thus yields a lazier training regime [d110208s0p0]. Task similarity modulates a transition from a low-forgetting lazy regime to a rich feature-learning regime with significant forgetting, so measures of task similarity (e.g., covariance or subspace alignment) change whether width increases help by shifting this transition point [d110208s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which concrete training protocols and hyperparameter regimes (for example: constant vs decaying learning rates, cyclic or warm restarts, minibatch sizes including single-sample SGD, number of epochs per task, and optimizer choice such as SGD vs momentum vs Adam) have been shown to amplify or diminish overparameterization advantages in linear continual-learning setups?
sub_answers.text: Analyses consider constant, intra-task decaying, and continuously decaying learning-rate schedules and show that restarting learning-rate decay at task boundaries affects propagation of historical sample perturbations and thus forgetting [d132661s0p0]. Single-pass Shuffle SGD dynamics under convex objectives have been analyzed to produce explicit upper bounds on expected final forgetting, highlighting the role of optimizer and single-pass protocols in continual setups [d131842s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: In linear continual learning, how do different memory/rehearsal strategies (including fixed-size replay buffers, reservoir sampling, prioritized replay, generative replay, and storing sufficient statistics) interact with model overparameterization—can replay of a given size replace width increases, and what are proven or empirical trade-offs between rehearsal capacity and parameter count?
sub_answers.text: Retaining representative samples via principled sample-compression replay can mitigate catastrophic forgetting and yields computable generalization bounds in continual learning [d106358s0p0]. Methods that avoid rehearsal buffers by using parameter-efficient memories or prompts can achieve competitive performance without rehearsal, indicating that rehearsal is not strictly necessary to match some rehearsal-based baselines [d72625s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Across empirical studies on linear sequential tasks, how do overparameterization benefits scale as the number of tasks grows—what are the reported breakpoints where additional width no longer improves average task error, how does performance decay with task count for fixed width, and how do factors like task heterogeneity, sample budget per task, and network width-to-task ratio determine these scalability limits?
sub_answers.text: Theoretical bounds on expected forgetting explicitly include the total number of tasks, showing that task count enters forgetting bounds and affects performance scaling [d132661s0p0]. Per-task data amount, task similarity, and task ordering enter forgetting bounds and determine empirical trends as task count grows [d131842s0p0]. Optimal performance occurs at a critical level of feature learning that depends on task non-stationarity and transfers across model scales, so width-to-task scaling limits depend on task heterogeneity and sample budgets per task [d110208s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Provide a precise, formal definition and mathematical formulation of "linear continual learning" for a sequence of tasks: specify the model class (linear predictors), learning protocol (sequential task presentation, no task labels, fine-tuning vs online update), loss functions, and the objective used to evaluate continual performance across tasks.
sub_answers.text: Linear continual learning uses linear predictors w in R^d mapping inputs x to predictions w^T x and learns a sequence of tasks presented sequentially without revisiting earlier task data in a single pass or via fine-tuning updates [d131842s0p0]. The learning protocol analyzed includes online single-pass updates such as Shuffle SGD and fine-tuning under convex objectives, where each task t supplies a dataset D_t and the learner updates parameters incrementally on arriving tasks [d131842s0p0]. Loss functions are standard convex losses (e.g., squared loss for regression, logistic or other convex classification losses) evaluated per-task, and the continual objective is to minimize cumulative or final expected loss across all tasks, often formalized via an upper bound on expected final forgetting after the last task [d131842s0p0]. Analyses consider both strongly convex and general convex objectives and measure performance of the final predictor on earlier tasks after sequential updates as the main evaluation criterion [d131842s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Define catastrophic forgetting in the setting of sequentially trained linear models and list concrete, quantitative metrics used to measure it: include formulas for forgetting, backward transfer, accuracy drop per task, parameter-change-based measures (e.g., projection of weight updates), and any closed-form expressions available for linear least-squares or ridge regression.
sub_answers.text: Catastrophic forgetting is quantified as the increase in expected loss on an earlier task when evaluated after learning subsequent tasks, often formalized as expected final forgetting, i.e., the expected excess loss on a past task at the end of training relative to its loss when that task was learned [d131842s0p0]. Backward transfer (BWT) and forward transfer (FWT) are defined as task-to-task performance changes where BWT measures the change in earlier-task performance after learning later tasks and FWT measures improvement on future tasks due to past learning [d118140s0p0]. Parameter-change-based measures include projections of weight updates onto principal optimizer directions and the magnitude of movement relative to a cone-like basin of good solutions, with empirical evidence that travel along a few top principal directions can quickly move parameters outside the solution region and produce forgetting [d63301s0p0]. Theoretical analyses produce explicit upper bounds on expected final forgetting for convex objectives, linking forgetting quantitatively to per-task data amounts, task similarity, and task ordering, which serve as closed-form or computable measures in linear/convex settings [d131842s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Summarize empirical findings that connect model width or total parameter count to the amount of forgetting in linear networks: cite specific experimental setups (synthetic teacher–student tasks, permuted/multitask MNIST, Gaussian features), describe observed scaling behaviors or plots (forgetting vs width/parameters), and note when wider models show increased, decreased, or nonmonotonic forgetting.
sub_answers.text: Empirical studies report that trends predicted by convex and linear theory about forgetting also appear in neural network experiments such as Split-CIFAR-100 and Permuted-MNIST, showing qualitative agreement between theory and practice for how training dynamics affect forgetting as model and data conditions vary [d131842s0p0]. Analyses of optimizer trajectories in overparameterized models find that the region of near-optimal performance resembles a cone that expands along the convergence direction, and that movement along a few top principal directions of the trajectory can rapidly drive parameters out of this cone and induce forgetting [d63301s0p0]. Experiments linking model width or parameter count explicitly to forgetting are studied within linear, overparameterized, or NTK regimes to understand how increasing parameterization changes dynamics, though specific numeric scaling laws or plots are reported in those analytic and empirical comparisons rather than summarized here [d131842s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: List and explain theoretical frameworks and analytical tools used to study overparameterization and forgetting in linear models: include Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) limits, linear regression/least-squares and ridge regression analyses, teacher–student models, random matrix theory, gradient-flow dynamics, and any theorems that relate parameter count, initialization, and training dynamics to forgetting.
sub_answers.text: Theoretical frameworks used include analysis in linear regression and least-squares/ridge regression regimes, overparameterized limits and Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) approximations, and teacher–student stylized models to obtain tractable predictions about forgetting and transfer [d131842s0p0]. Analytical tools include deriving explicit upper bounds on expected forgetting for strongly convex and general convex objectives, studying gradient-flow and SGD dynamics, and characterizing optimizer trajectory principal directions to relate parameter movement to loss degradation [d131842s0p0][d63301s0p0]. Other techniques invoked in these analyses include random matrix and high-dimensional statistical tools to handle overparameterization effects and optimization geometry, and constrained optimization formulations to reason about positive forward and backward transfer via task similarity and mask/subspace constraints [d118140s0p0][d63301s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: In the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) limit, how are the training dynamics of heavily overparameterized linear models and linearized neural networks described in terms of kernel regression: which kernel governs function updates, how do the NTK eigenvalues and eigenvectors determine convergence rates and generalization, and how does linearization about initialization change when width → ∞?
sub_answers.text: In the infinite-width (NTK) limit, training dynamics of heavily overparameterized models are described by kernel regression using the Neural Tangent Kernel that governs function updates under gradient descent [d50452s0p0][d59640s0p0]. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the NTK determine convergence rates and which function components learn faster, with eigenvalue decay controlling effective function class and generalization properties [d59851s0p0][d102015s0p0]. Linearizing the network about initialization becomes exact as width tends to infinity because the NTK converges to a deterministic limit, so the linearized (first-order) dynamics match the full network dynamics in that limit [d59640s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: When the number of parameters in a linear regression model is increased beyond the number of training dimensions, how does the dimensionality of the solution manifold (nullspace) grow, how many distinct interpolating solutions exist, and how do typical solutions (e.g., minimum-norm, ridge, or random-parameter solutions) decompose into projections onto task-relevant feature subspaces versus the nullspace?
sub_answers.text: Over-parameterized networks can fit any finite training sample perfectly, implying the existence of many interpolating solutions when parameters exceed training dimensions [d59819s0p0]. Gradient-descent training with early stopping on such over-parameterized models yields predictors whose statistical rates match those of the corresponding kernel (NTK) regression, indicating typical GD solutions align with the kernel-induced function projection rather than arbitrary interpolants [d102015s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Quantitatively, how do measures of alignment between task feature directions—such as cosine similarity, principal angles, or subspace overlap fraction—affect interference between tasks in linear models: what is the relationship between feature overlap and gradient correlation, cross-task error transfer, and how much orthogonalization (or decorrelation) is needed to reduce interference to a specified level?
sub_answers.text: A data-dependent kernel can reduce approximation error when task targets align with the data geometry, so greater alignment between feature directions and data geometry improves task-specific approximation and can thus change cross-task interactions [d120775s0p0]. Transformations that amplify the input Gram matrix condition number (e.g., linearized attention cubing the condition number) increase influence malleability and sensitivity to data perturbations, thereby increasing cross-task interference and transfer under perturbation [d120775s0p0]. The eigenvalue decay and eigenfunctions of kernels determine which directions are favored by learning and thus control how overlap in feature directions maps to shared or distinct learned components [d59851s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Through which mechanisms does the implicit bias of gradient descent in overparameterized linear models (e.g., convergence to minimum-norm or minimum-ℓ2 solutions, trajectory-dependent parameter selection, and effects of step size, momentum, and early stopping) determine how well parameters retain solutions learned on earlier tasks during sequential training, and how do these biases predict catastrophic forgetting versus preservation?
sub_answers.text: Gradient descent with appropriate training schedules (notably early stopping) biases over-parameterized models toward kernel-regression-like solutions and thus dictates which components of earlier-task solutions are retained during sequential training [d102015s0p0]. The implicit selection of particular interpolants or regularized solutions depends on training trajectory and scaling choices, and improper scaling of initialization can shrink trained network outputs, altering preservation of prior solutions [d59819s0p0]. The NTK-limit convergence of random initializations to a deterministic kernel implies that these implicit biases can be characterized by the corresponding kernel dynamics in the wide limit [d59640s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: For which degrees of task similarity (e.g., orthogonal labels vs. overlapping feature subspaces) and measured subspace overlap metrics (canonical correlation, subspace angle) does increasing model width or parameter count stop reducing interference between tasks during sequential training?
sub_answers.text: Increasing model width only reduces interference when it suppresses feature learning and moves the model toward a lazy/linearized regime rather than a rich feature-learning regime [d110208s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Through which mechanisms do shifts in label priors, time-varying input covariance matrices, or deliberately ordered adversarial task curricula (e.g., alternating oppositely-correlated tasks) negate the protective effects of large models on forgetting, and what empirical metrics (accuracy drift, forgetting index, Fisher overlap) quantify this failure?
sub_answers.text: Time-varying input covariances and task non-stationarity produce gradient interference across sequential tasks that undermines the protective effect of large, lazy models and increases catastrophic forgetting [d82725s0p0][d110208s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What are the formal failure cases in theory when training departs from NTK/linearized-gradient assumptions—such as finite-width fluctuations, feature learning regimes, or non-quadratic losses—and how do these lead to loss of guarantees (no convergence, increased interference, spurious minima)?
sub_answers.text: Theoretical guarantees tied to NTK or linearized-gradient (lazy) assumptions break down when training departs into finite-width fluctuations and feature-learning (rich) regimes, producing increased forgetting and qualitative changes in dynamics [d110208s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which experiments and datasets provide concrete counterexamples where simply scaling parameters (wider/deeper networks, more neurons) does not improve or worsens continual learning outcomes—cite task pairs, model families, and measured metrics where overparameterization fails?
sub_answers.text: Systematic experiments demonstrate that simply scaling width does not uniformly improve continual learning: increasing width helps only insofar as it reduces feature learning, and models in the rich regime exhibit significant forgetting despite larger parameter counts [d110208s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: In sequential-task linear models, how do different measures of task relatedness (e.g., cosine similarity of task weight vectors, shared feature subspaces, or covariance matrices) affect when and why highly overparameterized networks reduce catastrophic forgetting or improve transfer?
sub_answers.text: When task weight vectors have higher cosine similarity or tasks share feature subspaces, increased overparameterization can worsen feature learning and thus increase forgetting unless the model operates in a lazy regime with reduced feature learning [d110208s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which specific optimization and training regimes (for example: stepwise vs. cyclical learning-rate schedules, varying mini-batch sizes, momentum/Adam vs SGD, and single-epoch streaming versus multiple-epoch rehearsal) change the empirical impact of overparameterization on continual-learning performance in linear or kernel setting?
sub_answers.text: Restarting or varying learning-rate decay at task boundaries changes propagation of historical perturbations and thus affects how overparameterization influences forgetting across schedules like constant, intra-task decaying, and continuously decaying learning rates [d132661s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: To what extent can explicit memory mechanisms (replay buffers, reservoir sampling, generative replay) replicate or augment the performance gains attributed to overparameterization in linear continual-learning experiments, and which quantitative metrics (memory size, replay frequency, error decomposition) demonstrate substitution versus complementarity?
sub_answers.text: Explicit sample-retention mechanisms that keep representative past examples can mitigate forgetting and produce computable upper bounds on generalization loss, thereby reproducing some benefits of capacity by preserving past-task information [d106358s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Across empirical papers and benchmarks, how does the improvement from increasing parameter count scale as the number of sequential tasks grows (e.g., plateau points, diminishing returns, required overparameterization factor per task), and what task sequences or dataset properties cause those scalability limits?
sub_answers.text: There is a transition modulated by task similarity where models exit an effectively lazy regime with low forgetting to enter a rich regime with significant forgetting, implying diminishing returns from increasing width when task non-stationarity pushes the model into rich feature learning [d110208s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Provide a precise, formal definition of “linear continual learning” for sequential-task training settings: specify the model class (fully linear networks, linear predictors, or linearized networks around initialization), the training protocol (tasks presented one at a time, potentially without revisiting data), the objective (per-task loss, cumulative loss, online vs offline optimization), and how task boundaries and distribution shifts are modeled in the definition.
sub_answers.text: Linear continual learning studies sequential-task training where the model class is linear or linearized predictors, including fully linear networks or linearized networks around initialization, trained on a sequence of tasks presented one at a time without revisiting past task data in the online single-pass setup [d131842s0p0]. The training protocol consists of processing tasks sequentially with SGD or Shuffle SGD, possibly under strongly convex or general convex objectives, and may be either online (single pass) or iterative per task depending on the analysis [d131842s0p0]. The objective is typically a per-task loss minimized during its presentation, with interest in final or cumulative generalization loss after subsequent tasks rather than joint offline optimization over all tasks [d131842s0p0][d132661s0p0]. Task boundaries and distribution shifts are modeled by distinct tasks presented in sequence, with task similarity and ordering (including shifts in population data covariances and their eigenstructures) entering theoretical bounds on forgetting [d131842s0p0][d96673s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Explain what is meant by catastrophic forgetting in the context of linear models trained sequentially and list specific, quantifiable measures used in the literature (e.g., per-task accuracy drop after subsequent tasks, average forgetting, backward transfer metrics, change in task loss, overlap of weight/feature subspaces, projection of learned parameters onto previous-task solution subspaces), including formulas or procedures for computing these metrics.
sub_answers.text: Catastrophic forgetting is the degradation in performance on earlier tasks after training on later tasks, measured as increases in earlier task loss or decreases in earlier task accuracy following subsequent training [d132661s0p0]. One used decomposition distinguishes intra-task and cross-task generalization gaps and empirical forgetting, allowing expected population forgetting to be bounded via algorithmic stability analyses of SGD [d132661s0p0]. Quantifiable measures include per-task accuracy drop after later tasks and average forgetting or backward transfer metrics computed as differences between performance on a task immediately after training it and performance on that task after training further tasks, which correspond to changes in task loss or accuracy over the sequence [d132661s0p0]. Analyses also relate forgetting to changes in optimization trajectories and cumulative gradient alignment along the trajectory, which can be operationalized by measuring overlap or projections of subsequent gradients/parameters onto subspaces spanned by previous-task solutions [d132661s0p0][d63301s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Summarize empirical findings that connect model width or total parameter count to the amount of forgetting observed in linear neural networks or linearized models: cite experiments on wide vs narrow linear MLPs, random feature models, and linear models in the interpolation/overparameterized regime; report observed trends (less/more forgetting, double-descent-like behavior, dependence on regularization or task similarity) and note typical experimental setups (datasets, number of sequential tasks, metrics reported).
sub_answers.text: Empirical studies in linear settings report that overparameterized and wide linear models or linearized models can exhibit different forgetting behavior compared to underparameterized models, with analyses covering both underparameterized and overparameterized regimes via SGD [d96673s0p0]. Experiments show that task ordering and the spectrum of population data covariances matter, for example sequences where tasks with larger covariance eigenvalues are trained later tend to increase forgetting in sufficiently large-data regimes [d96673s0p0]. Simulations on linear regression and complementary experiments on deep networks validate theoretical trends linking step size, task order, and parameterization to forgetting, and comparisons between wide and narrow models are used to probe interpolation/overparameterized effects on forgetting [d96673s0p0]. The reported empirical setups include sequential tasks evaluated by measures such as task loss and accuracy after subsequent tasks and synthetic or benchmark simulations to confirm theoretical predictions across regimes [d96673s0p0][d131842s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: List and briefly describe the theoretical frameworks and analytical tools used to study overparameterization effects in linear models for sequential training: include Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) and its linearized dynamics, closed-form analyses of linear least-squares and ridge regression under sequential updates, random matrix theory results on eigenvalue spectra and memorization, mean-field or lazy/feature-learning distinctions, and any known generalization or stability bounds that relate parameter count to forgetting or transfer.
sub_answers.text: Theoretical tools used include analysis in linear and overparameterized regimes and Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) or linearized dynamics to connect parameterization to forgetting behavior [d131842s0p0]. Closed-form analyses of linear least-squares and linear regression under SGD, including both underparameterized and overparameterized cases, are used to derive explicit bounds on expected forgetting [d96673s0p0]. Algorithmic stability frameworks for SGD decompose forgetting into generalization gaps and empirical forgetting and produce bounds that track how sample perturbations propagate through subsequent tasks under various learning-rate schedules [d132661s0p0]. Convex-objective analyses (strongly convex and general convex) and bounds that expose dependence on per-task data size, task similarity, task ordering, and cumulative gradient alignment are also employed to relate parameter counts and training dynamics to forgetting [d131842s0p0][d132661s0p0][d96673s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: In the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) limit, how do the kernel eigenvalues, initialization scale, and linearization approximation determine convergence rates, mode-wise learning dynamics, and generalization for overparameterized linear and linearized neural models?
sub_answers.text:
In the NTK limit the network training dynamics reduce to kernel regression governed by the NTK eigenvalues which set mode-wise learning rates through their magnitudes and decay rates [d50452s0p0].
The eigenvalue decay rate determines which function components are learned faster and which contribute more to generalization via the RKHS smoothness induced by the kernel [d59851s0p0].
Initialization scale and the linearization approximation enable this kernel regime equivalence for sufficiently wide models and thereby fix convergence rates to those implied by the NTK spectrum rather than by feature learning dynamics [d50452s0p0].
When the linearization holds, generalization and mode-wise dynamics follow the NTK eigenstructure so that components aligned with large eigenvalues converge quickly and dominate final predictions [d59851s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: As the number of parameters grows in linear regression, how do changes in nullspace dimension, matrix rank, and degrees of freedom alter the multiplicity of solutions, the form of the minimum-norm/least-squares solution, and the size of projections of solutions onto specified task subspaces?
sub_answers.text:
As parameters grow the model nullspace dimension increases and the parameter-to-equation rank deficit grows, producing a multiplicity of solutions consistent with the training data [d96673s0p0].
The increase in nullspace and reduced effective matrix rank leads gradient-based training in the infinite-width/kernel regime to select specific solutions such as minimum-norm or kernel-regression solutions determined by the optimization dynamics and implicit bias [d50452s0p0].
The minimum-norm or least-squares solution in overparameterized linear regression is characterized by projection onto the row space of the data and nulling components in the nullspace, changing the form of solutions as degrees of freedom increase [d96673s0p0].
Larger nullspaces reduce the magnitude of projections of learned solutions onto task-specific subspaces unless the optimization bias explicitly preserves those components through initialization or regularization choices [d96673s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Quantitatively, how do pairwise angles, cosine similarities, or subspace principal angles between task feature vectors (or their span) govern interference and cross-talk — for example, how does increasing orthogonality or reducing subspace overlap change projection residuals and interference magnitudes?
sub_answers.text:
Pairwise angles and cosine similarities between task feature vectors enter interference through the input Gram or covariance geometry, with larger angles (greater orthogonality) reducing cross-talk and interference magnitudes [d120775s0p0].
Reducing subspace overlap lowers projection residuals onto other tasks because the Gram-induced kernel amplifies directions aligned across tasks and attenuates orthogonal directions, thereby decreasing interference when tasks are more orthogonal [d120775s0p0].
Architectures with localized parameter support can induce structural rank deficits in the cross-task NTK, which reduces effective subspace overlap and hence cross-task interference via reduced coupling in the NTK Gram between tasks [d123667s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which implicit biases of gradient descent (e.g., selection of minimum ℓ2-norm solutions, trajectory dependence on learning rate and initialization, early-stopping effects) explain why overparameterized linear models preferentially retain or erase parameter components associated with earlier tasks during sequential training?
sub_answers.text:
Gradient descent in overparameterized linear models has an implicit bias toward minimum ℓ2-norm solutions, which preserves components in the row space while nulling components in the parameter nullspace, affecting retention of earlier-task components [d50452s0p0].
Training trajectory, including step size and initialization scale, affects which components are retained or erased because these algorithmic parameters interact with task ordering and NTK/eigenvalue structure to determine how quickly components are learned or forgotten [d96673s0p0].
Early stopping and finite-time dynamics can prevent full convergence along slow eigenmodes, leading to preferential retention of components associated with large-eigenvalue directions and erasure of small-eigenvalue components tied to earlier tasks [d59851s0p0].
Appropriate choice of step size mitigates forgetting in both underparameterized and overparameterized regimes by modifying the temporal weighting of mode updates along gradient descent trajectories [d96673s0p0].
